tool.name: SurfaceAreaRatio
tool.summary: Calculates the true three-dimensional surface area of the terrain within each DEM cell using the 8-triangle method of Jenness (2004), plus the surface ratio (surface area / flat area, a topographic roughness index) and the planimetric (flat) cell area. Any combination of the three outputs; correct on geographic (latitude/longitude) rasters.
tool.usage:
The planimetric ("flat") area of a landscape understates how much land surface actually exists wherever the terrain slopes: a steep hillside contains more surface than the map area beneath it. This tool estimates the true surface area of each cell with the 8-triangle method of Jenness (2004): eight three-dimensional triangles connect the cell center to eight points interpolated on the cell boundary (the four edge midpoints and the four corners), each triangle's area is computed from its three 3-D side lengths with Heron's formula, and their sum is the cell's surface area. The SURFACE RATIO output divides that area by the cell's flat area - a unitless roughness index that equals 1 on level ground and grows with slope and terrain convolution - and the FLAT AREA output is the planimetric cell area itself. Choose any combination of the three outputs (at least one is required).
Corner elevation interpolation offers two methods. The ORIGINAL method (the default, matching the legacy DEM Surface Tools) sets each corner elevation to the midpoint of the focal and diagonal cell centers. The CORNER AVERAGE method instead averages all four cells that share the corner - the true bilinear estimate of the elevation at that point, and therefore a more accurate interpolation (the edge midpoints are already exact in this sense). On a perfectly planar slope the two methods give identical results; they differ only where the surface curves. Use the original method to reproduce legacy results exactly; use the corner average for the more faithful estimate.
Unlike planar tools, this tool is accurate for DEMs in geographic coordinate systems: all distances are spheroidal chord lengths recomputed for every row of the raster, and cell areas are true spheroid areas at each row's latitude - so surface areas, ratios, and flat areas are all correct at any latitude without projecting the DEM first. Projected DEMs use constant planar cell dimensions. Elevation units are read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when one is defined (geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters); otherwise the tool asks you to choose meters or feet.
Outputs may be saved into a geodatabase or as files in a folder. In a folder, a name typed WITHOUT an extension is saved as a GeoTIFF (.tif, with a .tfw world file) - the legacy Esri GRID format is never used, so its 13-character name limit no longer applies. You may also type an explicit extension (.tif or .img) to choose the file format; formats that cannot store 32-bit floating-point values (such as .png or .bmp) are rejected with a clear error.
Optional local detrending (Dilts et al. 2023). The surface ratio is a "first generation" ruggedness index in the terms of Dilts et al. (2023): it is correlated with slope, so a smooth but steep hillside scores as rough. Turning on "Remove smooth topography first" subtracts a circular neighborhood mean of the DEM (the smoothing radius you set, default 1.5 cells = a 3 x 3 mean) before the surface-area computation, leaving only the fine-scale surface variation. The surface RATIO then becomes Dilts's "local" surface-area-ratio variant (SAPR-L), a third-generation index that measures fine-scale surface roughness independent of both slope and smooth folding. In this mode the surface ratio is the meaningful roughness output; the surface-area and flat-area outputs describe the detrended residual surface rather than the original terrain, so they are rarely of interest. (Dilts et al. define three generations of ruggedness index: first generation = elevation variability such as the surface ratio or TRI, correlated with slope; second generation = aspect diversity such as VRM or the Arc-Chord Ratio, slope-independent but fooled by smooth folds; third generation = this local, detrended family, isolating surface roughness itself.)
Surface area and surface ratio are NoData wherever any cell of the 3 x 3 neighborhood is NoData, and on the outer edge of the raster. The flat area raster is written for every cell (it does not depend on elevations). Outputs are floating point and carry statistics and a histogram so they render correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step; pyramids are built with bilinear resampling.
By default each output matches the input grid exactly (same extent, cell size, and coordinate system). Honored environments: Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System, all applied as finishing steps to the computed rasters - the extent clips (with the snap raster aligning the clip window), the cell size resamples, and the output coordinate system reprojects. The Mask environment is not honored, and pyramids are always built with bilinear resampling regardless of the Pyramid environment.
Reference: Jenness, J. S. 2004. Calculating landscape surface area from digital elevation models. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute surface areas from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk.

The three-dimensional surface area of the terrain within each cell, in the chosen surface area units. Larger values indicate steeper or more convoluted terrain. At least one of the three outputs must be specified.
The areal units of the surface area raster: Sq. Meters, Sq. Feet, Hectares, Acres, Sq. Kilometers, or Sq. Miles.

The ratio of each cell's three-dimensional surface area to its planimetric (flat) area - a unitless topographic roughness index that equals 1 on level ground and increases with slope and terrain convolution. At least one of the three outputs must be specified.

The planimetric (map) area of each cell, in the chosen flat area units. Constant on projected rasters; varies by row on geographic rasters, where cell areas are computed on the spheroid and shrink toward the poles. Valid for every cell, including NoData areas of the DEM. At least one of the three outputs must be specified.
The areal units of the flat area raster: Sq. Meters, Sq. Feet, Hectares, Acres, Sq. Kilometers, or Sq. Miles.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say.

How the elevation at each corner of the cell is interpolated. "Diagonal midpoint (2 cells, original method)" averages the focal and diagonal cell centers, exactly matching the legacy DEM Surface Tools. "Corner average (4 cells)" averages all four cells that share the corner - the true bilinear estimate at that point, and a more accurate interpolation. The two methods are identical on a planar slope and differ only where the surface curves.

Turn on to locally detrend the DEM before the surface-area computation (Dilts et al. 2023): a circular neighborhood mean is subtracted from the DEM, leaving only the fine-scale surface variation, so smooth ridgelines and drainages no longer read as rough. The surface RATIO output then becomes Dilts's "local" variant (SAPR-L), a roughness index independent of both slope and smooth folding; the surface-area output describes the detrended residual surface (rarely of interest). Detrending changes the elevations only, so it has no effect on the flat-area output - and is therefore available only when a surface-area or surface-ratio output is specified. Off by default (the standard surface area and ratio).

The radius of the circular neighborhood mean used to smooth the DEM for detrending. The default, 1.5 cells, is exactly a 3 x 3 mean (the smoothing Dilts et al. 2023 used); larger radii remove broader-scale topography before the roughness is measured. Only used when detrending is on.

Units for the smoothing (detrending) radius: Cells, or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles) converted to cells from the cell size - planarly for projected rasters, geodesically per row for geographic rasters. Only used when detrending is on.

scriptExample.title: Surface Area and Ratio example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Surface area in acres plus the roughness ratio, with the improved corner interpolation.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\Tools\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") arcpy.jenness.SurfaceAreaRatio( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", out_area=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_SurfArea", out_ratio=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_SurfRatio", area_units="Acres", elev_units="Meters", corner_method="Corner average (4 cells)")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: True three-dimensional surface area, surface ratio (roughness), and planimetric cell area from a DEM via the 8-triangle method of Jenness (2004), with correct geodesic handling of geographic rasters and a choice of corner-interpolation methods.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Calculates the three-dimensional surface area of the terrain within each DEM cell using the 8-triangle method of Jenness (2004): eight 3-D triangles connect the cell center to interpolated boundary points, with areas from Heron's formula. Optional outputs (at least one): surface area (choice of areal units), surface ratio (surface/flat, a roughness index), and flat planimetric cell area. Corner elevations use the original diagonal-midpoint interpolation or a more accurate 4-cell corner average (identical on planar slopes). On geographic DEMs all distances and cell areas are computed per row on the spheroid. Reference: Jenness, J. S. 2004. Calculating landscape surface area from digital elevation models. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839.
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Method: Jenness, J. S. 2004. Calculating landscape surface area from digital elevation models. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839. Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Surface Area and Ratio. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife Tools for ArcGIS Pro. Available at: http://www.jennessent.com.
